headline: Retail investors systematically sell at 52-week highs, creating liquidity that institutional investors exploit to build positions cheaply — a major source of institutional outperformance
reasoning: Andrew Grant references his own published research showing that retail investors systematically sell when market sentiment is highly positive (i.e. at or near 52-week highs) and also sell when sentiment turns negative. Institutional investors take the other side of these trades in both directions, profiting from the predictable behavioural errors of retail participants. The increased selling pressure from retail investors opens up liquidity and tightens spreads for institutions. Grant argues this dynamic has been responsible for a large portion of institutional outperformance over retail investors.
quote: I think that is part of it. And also the fact that, you know, there is increased selling pressure from individual investors. It opens up, you know, more liquidity, smaller spreads for institutional investors. It's a it's a great time for institutions to take advantage of the free money that's out there.
episode_title: Wealthy & Wise | the most dangerous number in investing

headline: Disposition effect drives retail selling at highs: investors lock in gains without knowing fundamental value, using price paid as their only reference point
reasoning: Andrew Grant explains that the disposition effect — the tendency to sell winners and hold losers — is the primary driver of retail selling near 52-week highs. Investors anchor to their purchase price; when the current price exceeds it, the impulse is to lock in the gain. The flip side is 'get-even-itis', where investors hold losing positions waiting to recover to break-even. He emphasises that retail investors lack the valuation tools to judge whether a price is fundamentally cheap or expensive, so they rely on the 52-week range as a crude barometer, using it as a sell signal without any fundamental basis.
quote: One of the most common ways in which people make decisions is I bought the stock at a price, and now it's currently worth more than what I paid for it. So this is something called the disposition effect. It means I want to sell the stock because I'm going to lock in this game, right? So making a profit, that seems to be what we're all aiming for in the stock price... what we don't know when it comes to trading stocks and what individual investors aren't really good at is understanding how much should the stock be worth, right? The stock could be worth $32 on the stock market. I'm like, is that a good price? Is that a bad price? I don't know, right. All I can say is it's worth more than what I paid for. And I can see relative to where the stock's been over the past year here. It's at a high price time to sell. So that's the logic. It's like the barometer the temperature. The temperature is higher than where it's been. Now it's time to sell.

headline: Focusing on dividend income and whole-portfolio thinking reduces purchase-price anchoring and improves long-term decision-making
reasoning: Andrew Grant argues that investors can counter purchase-price anchoring by shifting focus to two things: the ongoing dividend income generated by holdings (which reduces the urge to sell quickly), and the portfolio-level rationale for each position rather than treating each stock as a standalone P&L. He notes that viewing stocks in isolation causes investors to underestimate the diversification and risk-offsetting value each holding provides, leading to sub-optimal sell decisions driven by arbitrary price levels.
quote: I think to add to his point, you know, there are other things we can think about that aren't related to the purchase price. We can think about if I'm buying stocks, perhaps focus on the dividends that you're getting from the stocks and hold that as part of the rationale for buying the stock and holding the stock. So you're not likely to want to sell out quickly if the stock is generating some profits for you on a, you know, on an annual or semi-annual basis. That's that's one way of sort of getting the purchase price out of your mind. And secondly, I think, right. Well, what did I buy the stock for in the first place? Is it to make a quick profit or is it to, you know, generate a portfolio for the long run? And I think the other side of this is when we focus on separating out our assets like stock A, stock B stock, see as if to say their individual investments. And don't think of our whole portfolio, then we're ignoring why we might want to hold different pieces of the pie, because some of them will allow us to diversify our risk or offset other risks that we might be holding.

headline: Individual investors consistently mistimed — buying after runs and replacing sold stocks with ones that go up even more; doing the opposite of the crowd may offer an edge
reasoning: Andrew Grant notes that individual investors lack the full information set and analytical capability of professional investors, leaving them working with limited data. Behavioural finance research shows retail investors are poor at timing: they tend to buy stocks that have already risen too much, and when they sell, they replace those positions with stocks that subsequently appreciate even further. This implies a contrarian signal — buying what individuals want to sell and selling what they want to buy may generate excess returns. The utility derived from selling at a profit also reinforces the disposition effect, making investors reluctant to sell at a loss even when it would be rational.
quote: Research in behavioral finance shows that individuals aren't good at timing their decisions. Right. So in other words, they'll buy stocks after they've gone up too much. And then they'll replace stocks in their portfolio with stocks then end up going up even more. So it ends up that if you followed what the individual does and do the exact opposite, so you buy the stocks they want to sell and you sell the stocks they want to buy, there's probably some likelihood of earning a profit.

headline: Sydney property is an example of a market where waiting for a pullback from 'high' prices has persistently cost investors over 30 years — there is no shortage of investment opportunities elsewhere
reasoning: Andrew Grant uses the Sydney property market over the last 30 years as an analogy for the danger of waiting for a pullback that never comes. He argues that prices appearing high 20 years ago did not mean investors should have stayed out. His broader point is that investors should not be paralysed by the fear of buying at a high, as there is no shortage of other investment opportunities, and dwelling on missed past opportunities is unproductive.
quote: If you looked at the property market in the last 30 years and say, okay, well the house prices in Sydney are quite high 20 years ago, I better stay out of it and wait till they come down. I mean, when, when are you going to join in? I suppose there's one question, but then secondly it's like, okay, you, you could have bought and you should have bought. Okay. No, no, no use crying over spilt milk. Get in.
episode_title: Wealthy & Wise | the most dangerous number in investing
